hints: Focus on what a catalytic converter is for, turning the most harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones.
Notice that reaction 2 turns toxic CO and NO into harmless N2 and CO2, which is exactly the redox job of the converter.
Check whether unburnt petrol also gets oxidised in the converter, and whether sulfur chemistry in reaction 3 plays any part there.
walkthrough:
**Recall the job of the converter**

Think of the converter as a clean-up unit after the engine. It oxidises toxic CO and unburnt hydrocarbons to $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and it reduces $\text{NO}_x$ to harmless $\text{N}_2$.

Key idea:
$$\text{CO, C}_x\text{H}_y \text{ oxidised, NO}_x \text{ reduced}$$

**Test reaction 1**

Reaction 1 is complete combustion of octane, a model for petrol:
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18} + 12\tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 8\text{CO}_2 + 9\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Unburnt hydrocarbons leaving the engine are oxidised like this on the platinum and palladium catalyst, so 1 is correct.

**Test reaction 2 and 3**

Reaction 2 is the classic reduction of nitrogen monoxide by carbon monoxide:
$$2\text{NO} + 2\text{CO} \rightarrow \text{N}_2 + 2\text{CO}_2$$
This removes two pollutants at once on the rhodium catalyst, so 2 is correct.

Reaction 3 involves $\text{SO}_3$ to $\text{SO}_2$ interconversion. Sulfur compounds are not cleaned this way in a petrol converter, so 3 is incorrect. Therefore 1 and 2 only.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes all three reactions. Reactions 1 and 2 are correct converter chemistry, but reaction 3 involving NO with SO3 is not a catalytic converter reaction.
options.B: Correct because both 1 and 2 occur. Reaction 1 shows oxidation of unburnt hydrocarbon to CO2 and H2O, and reaction 2 shows reduction of NO by CO to N2 and CO2. These are the two key functions of the converter.
options.C: Incorrect because it includes reaction 3 and omits reaction 1. Reaction 3 does not occur in the converter, while oxidation of hydrocarbons in reaction 1 definitely does.
options.D: Incorrect if it states 2 only. Many students remember the NO to N2 reduction but forget that oxidation of CO and unburnt hydrocarbons also happens on the same catalyst, so reaction 1 is missed.
